overseer: One who oversees; a superintendent; a supervisor; as, an overseer of a mill; specifically, one or certain public officers; as, an overseer of the poor; an overseer of highways.
overinform: To inform, fill, or animate, excessively. Johnson.
ovalbumen: The albumin from white of eggs; egg albumin; -- in distinction from serum albumin. See Albumin.
overwork: 1. To work beyond the strength; to cause to labor too much or too long; to tire excessively; as, to overwork a horse. 2. To fill too full of work; to crowd with labor. | To work too much, or beyond one's strength.
oviparity: Generatuon by means of ova. See Generation.
overshade: To cover with shade; to render dark or gloomy; to overshadow. Shak.
overthwart: 1. Having a transverse position; placed or situated across; hence, opposite. "Our overthwart neighbors." Dryden. 2. Crossing in kind or disposition; perverse; adverse; opposing. | Across; crosswise; transversely. "Y'clenched overthwart and endelong." Chaucer.
overgrassed: Overstocked, or overgrown, or covered, with grass. (old) Spenser.
overcount: To rate too high; to outnumber. Shak.
overpower: To excel or exceed in power; to cause to yield; to vanquish; to subdue; as, the light overpowers the eyes. "And overpower'd that gallant few." Wordsworth. Syn. -- To overbear; overcome; vanquish; defeat; crush; overwhelm; overthrow; rout; conquer; subdue.
ovaterotundate: Having a form intermediate between that of an egg and a sphere; roundly ovate.
ovateoblong: Oblong. with one end narrower than the other; ovato-oblong.
overshoot: 1. To shoot over or beyond. "Not to overshoot his game." South. 2. To pass swiftly over; to fly beyond. Hartle. 3. To exceed; as, to overshoot the truth. Cowper. To overshoot one's self, to venture… | To fly beyond the mark. Collier.
ovate: 1. Shaped like an egg, with the lower extremity broadest. 2. (Bot.) Having the shape of an egg, or of the longitudinal sectior of an egg, with the broader end basal. Gray.
overrule: 1. To rule over; to govern or determine by superior authority. 2. To rule or determine in a contrary way; to decide against; to abrogate or alter; as, God overrules the purposes of men; | To be superior or supreme in rulling or controlling; as, God rules and overrules. Shak.
overween: To think too highly or arrogantly; to regard one's own thinking or conclusions too highly; hence, to egotistic, arrogant, or rash, in opinion; to think conceitedly; to presume. They that overween, And at thy growing virtues fret their spleen. Milton.
overdevelop: To develop excessively; specif. (Photog.), to subject (a plate or film) too long to the developing process.
over: 1. Above, or higher than, in place or position, with the idea of covering; -- opposed to Ant: under; as, clouds are over our heads; the smoke rises over the city. | 1. From one side to another; from side to side; across; crosswise; as, a board, or a tree, a foot over, i. e., a foot in diameter. 2. From one person or place to another regarded as on the opposite…
overwax: To wax or grow too rapindly or too much. (old) R. of Gloucester.
oversell: 1. To sell for a higher price than; to exceed in selling price. One whose beauty Would oversell all Italy. Beau. & Fl. 2. To sell beyond means of delivery. [Brokers'Cant] Oversold market (Brokers' Cant), a market in which stocks or commodities have been sold "short" to such an extent that it is difficult to obtain them for delivery.
overpamper: To pamper excessively; to feed or dress too much. Dryton.
overturn: 1. To turn or throw from a basis, foundation, or position; to overset; as, to overturn a carriage or a building. 2. To subvert; to destroy; to overthrow. 3. To overpower; to conquer. Milton. Syn. | The act off overturning, or the state of being overturned or subverted; overthrow; as, an overturn of parties.
overmultiply: To multiply or increase too much; to repeat too often.
overmast: To furnish (a vessel) with too long or too heavy a mast or masts.
overbend: To bend to excess. | To bend over.
overlogical: Excessively logical; adhering too closely to the forms or rules of logic.
overhip: To pass over by, or as by a hop; to skip over; hence, to overpass. (old) "When the time is overhipt." Holland.
overblow: 1. To blow over, or be subdued. Spenser. 2. (Mus.) To force so much wind into a pipe that it produces an overtone, or a note higher than the natural note; thus, the upper octaves of a flute are… | To blow away; to dissipate by wind, or as by wind. When this cloud of sorrow's overblown. Waller.
overproduction: Excessive production; supply beyond the demand. J. S. Mill.
overstate: To state in too strong terms; to exaggerate. Fuller.
overlap: 1. The lapping of one thing over another; as, an overlap of six inches; an overlap of a slate on a roof. 2. (Geol.) An extension of geological beds above and beyond others, as in a conformable series of beds, when the upper beds extend over a wider space than the lower, either in one or in all directions.
overhold: To hold or value too highly; to estimate at too dear a rate. (old) Shak.
overhauling: A strict examination with a view to correction or repairs.
overruling: Exerting controlling power; as, an overruling Providence. -- O`ver*rul"ing*ly, adv.
overofficious: Too busy; too ready to intermeddle; too officious. Collier.
overbold: Excessively or presumptuously bold; impudent. Shak. -- O"ver*bold"ly, adv.
overperch: To perch upon; to fly over. (old) Shak.
overdrown: To wet or drench to excess. (old) W. Browne.
overheat: To heat to excess; to superheat. Cowper.
oviduct: A tube, or duct, for the passage of ova from the ovary to the exterior of the animal or to the part where further development takes place. In mammals the oviducts are also called Fallopian tubes.
ovipara: An artifical division of vertebrates, including those that lay eggs; -opposed to Vivipara.
overhandle: To handle, or use, too much; to mention too often. Shak.
overpicture: To surpass nature in the picture or representation of. (old) "O'erpicturing that Venus." Shak.
overpowering: Excelling in power; too powerful; irresistible. -- O`ver*pow"er*ing*ly, adv.
overflow: 1. To flow over; to cover woth, or as with, water or other fluid; to spread over; to inundate; to overwhelm. The northern nations overflowed all Christendom. Spenser. 2. To flow over the brim of; | 1. To run over the bounds. 2. To be superabundant; to abound. Rogers.
overnice: Excessively nice; fastidious. Bp. Hall. -- O"ver*nice"ly, adv. -- O"ver*nice"ness, n.
overtake: 1. To come up with in a course, pursuit, progress, or motion; to catch up with. Follow after the men; and when thou dost overtake them, say . . . Wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good. Gen. xliv. 4. He had him overtaken in his flight. Spenser. 2. To come upon from behind; to discover; to surprise; to capture; to overcome. If a man be overtaken in a fault. Gal. vi.
overshadow: 1. To throw a shadow, or shade, over; to darken; to obscure. There was a cloud that overshadowed them. Mark ix. 7. 2. Fig.: To cover with a superior influence. Milton.
overdate: To date later than the true or proper period. Milton.
overdraft: The act of overdrawing; also, the amount or sum overdrawn.
overthwartly: In an overthwart manner;across; also, perversely. (old) Peacham.
ovarial: Of or pertaining to an ovary.
overhent: To overtake. (old) So forth he went and soon them overhent. Spenser.
ovidian: Of or pertaining to the Latin poet Ovid; resembling the style of Ovid.
overmuch: Too much. -- adv. In too great a degree; too much. -- n. An excess; a surplus.
ovicell: One of the dilatations of the body wall of Bryozoa in which the ova sometimes undegro the first stages of their development. See Illust. of Chilostoma.
overbrim: To flow over the brim; to be so full as to overflow.
overtrading: The act or practice of buying goods beyond the means of payment; a glutting of the market.
overking: A king who has sovereignty over inferior kings or ruling princes. J. R. Green.
ovicular: Of or pertaining to an egg.
overbattle: Excessively fertile; bearing rank or noxious growths. (old) "Overbattle grounds." Hooker.
overcloud: To cover or overspread with clouds; to becloud; to overcast.
overthrow: 1. To throw over; to overturn; to upset; to turn upside down. His wife overthrew the table. Jer. Taylor. 2. To cause to fall or to fail; to subvert; to defeat; to make a ruin of; to destroy. | 1. The act of overthrowing; the state of being overthrow; ruin. Your sudden overthrow much rueth me. Spenser. 2. (a) (Baseball) The act of throwing a ball too high, as over a player's head.
overtrust: Excessive confidence. | To trust too much. Bp. Hall.
overbuilt: Having too many buildings; as, an overbuilt part of a town.
ovular: Relating or belonging to an ovule; as, an ovular growth.
overglaze: (a) Applied over the glaze; -- said of enamel paintings, which sometimes are seen to project from the surface of the ware. (b) Suitable for applying upon the glaze; -- said of vitrifiable colors used in ceramic decoration.
overcome: 1. To get the better of; to surmount; to conquer; to subdue; as, to overcome enemies in battle. This wretched woman overcome Of anguish, rather than of crime, hath been. Spenser. 2. To overflow; | To gain the superiority; to be victorious. Rev. iii. 21.
overfall: 1. A cataract; a waterfall. (old) 2. (Naut.) A turbulent surface of water, caused by strong currents setting over submerged ridges; also, a dangerous submerged ridge or shoal.
overjoy: To make excessively joyful; to gratify extremely.
oversea: Over the sea; abroad. Milton. Tennyson.
overfeed: To feed to excess; to surfeit.
overjump: To jump over; hence, to omit; to ignore. Marston.
overlive: To outlive. Sir P. Sidney. The culture of Northumbria overlived the term of its political supermacy. Earle. | To live too long, too luxuriously, or too actively. Milton. "Overlived in this close London life." Mrs. Browning.
overweener: One who overweens. The conceits of warmed or overweening brain. Locke.
overdye: To dye with excess of color; to put one color over (another). Shak.
overliness: The quality or state of being overly; carelessness. (old) Bp. Hall.
overbuy: 1. To buy too much. 2. To buy at too dear a rate. Dryden.
overmatch: 1. To be more than equal to or a match for; hence, to vanquish. Drayton. 2. To marry (one) to a superior. (old) Burton. | One superior in power; also, an unequal match; a contest in which one of the opponents is overmatched. Milton. D. Webster.
overexpose: To expose excessively; specif. (Photog.), to subject (a plate or film) too long to the actinic action of the light used in producing a picture. -- O`ver*ex*po"sure (#), n.
overcharge: 1. To charge or load too heavily; to burden; to oppress; to cloy. Sir W. Raleigh. 2. To fill too full; to crowd. Our language is overcharged with consonants. Addison. 3. To charge excessively; | 1. An excessive load or burden. 2. An excessive charge in an account.
overest: Uppermost; outermost. Full threadbare was his overeste courtepy. Chaucer.
ovicapsule: 1. (Anat) The outer layer of a Graafian follicle. 2. (Zoöl.) Same as Oötheca.
overhead: Aloft; above; in or attached to the ceiling or roof; in the story or upon the floor above; in the zenith. While overhead the moon Sits arbitress. Milton. Note: Also used adjectively; as, an overhead crane, gear, etc. Overhead engine, a vertical steam engine in which the cylinder stands above the crank.
overfull: Too full; filled to overflowing; excessively full; surfeited. Shak.
overground: Situated over or above ground; as, the overground portion of a plant.
overlash: To drive on rashly; to go to excess; hence, to exaggerate; to boast. (old) Barrow.
overskip: To skip or leap over; to treat with indifference. Shak.
overweigh: To exceed in weight; to overbalance; to weigh down. Drayton. Hooker.
overarch: To make or place an arch over; to hang over like an arch. "Brown with o'erarching shades." Pope.
overstrain: To strain one's self to excess. Dryden. | To stretch or strain too much; as to overstrain one's nerves. Ayliffe.
overprompt: Too prompt; too ready or eager; precipitate. -- O`ver*prompt"ness, n.
overslop: An outer garment, or slop. (old) Chaucer.
overbow: To bend or bow over; to bend in a contrary direction. (old) Fuller.
overhasty: Too hasty; precipitate; rash. -- O"ver*has"ti*ly, adv. -- O`ver*has"ti*ness, n.
overgrow: 1. To grow over; to cover with growth or herbage, esp. that which is rank. The green . . . is rough and overgrown. Sir W. Scott. 2. To grow beyond; to rise above; hence, to overcome; to oppress. | To grow beyond the fit or natural size; as, a huge, overgrown ox. L'Estrange.
ovology: That branch of natural history which treats of the origin and functions of eggs.
overpart: To give too important or difficult a part to. (old) B. Jonson.
overmagnify: To magnify too much. Bp. Hall.
overlabor: 1. To cause to labor excessively; to overwork. Dryden. 2. To labor upon excessively; to refine unduly.
ovisac: (a) A Graafian follicle; any sac containing an ovum or ova. (b) The inner layer of the fibrous wall of a Graafian follicle.
overmodest: Modest to excess; bashful. -- O"ver*mod"est*ly, adv.
overtax: To tax or to task too heavily.
ovule: (a) The rudiment of a seed. It grows from a placenta, and consists of a soft nucleus within two delicate coatings. The attached base of the ovule is the hilum, the coatings are united with the nucleus at the chalaza, and their minute orifice is the foramen. (b) An ovum.
overtitle: To give too high a title to.
oversnow: To cover with snow, or as with snow. (poetic) Shak. Dryden.
overmount: To mount over; to go higher than; to rise above.
ovaliform: Having the form of an egg; having a figure such that any section in the direction of the shorter diameter will be circular, and any in the direction of the longer diameter will be oval.
overhear: 1. To hear more of (anything) than was intended to be heard; to hear by accident or artifice. Shak. 2. To hear again. ShaK.
oviferous: Egg-bearing; -- applied particularly to certain receptacles, as in Crustacea, that retain the eggs after they have been excluded from the formative organs, until they are hatched.
overdo: 1. To do too much; to exceed what is proper or true in doing; to exaggerate; to carry too far. Anything so overdone is from the purpose of playing. Shak. 2. To overtask. or overtax; to fatigue; | To labor too hard; to do too much.
oviposit: To lay or deposit eggs; -- said esp. of insects.
oversman: 1. An overseer; a superintendent. 2. (Scots Law) An umpire; a third arbiter, appointed when two arbiters, previously selected, disagree.
overthwartness: The state of being overthwart; perverseness. (old) Lord Herbert.
override: 1. To ride over or across; to ride upon; to trample down. The carter overridden with [i. e., by] his cart. Chaucer. 2. To suppress; to destroy; to supersede; to annul; as, one low overrides another; to override a veto. 3. To ride beyond; to pass; to outride. (old) I overrode him on the way. Shak. 4. To ride too much; to ride, as a horse, beyond its strength.
ovarian: Of or pertaining to an ovary.
overdeal: The excess. (old) The overdeal in the price will be double. Holland.
ovulist: A believer in the theory (called encasement theory), current during the last century, that the egg was the real animal germ, and that at the time of fecundation the spermatozoa simply gave the impetus which caused the unfolding of the egg, in which all generations were inclosed one within the other. Also called ovist.
overpaint: To color or describe too strongly. Sir W. Raleigh.
ovary: 1. (Bot.) That part of the pistil which contains the seed, and in most flowering plants develops into the fruit. See Illust. of Flower. 2. (Zoöl. & Anat.) The essential female reproductive organ in which the ova are produced. See Illust. of Discophora.
ovolo: A round, convex molding. See Illust. of Column. Note: In Roman work it is usually a quarter circle in section; in Greek work it is flatter, and is equivalent to the echinus; that is, it has in section the elastic curve of the shell of the sea urchin. In mediæval architecture it is not distinguishable from the multitude of convex moldings, of all sections, which are used.
overdose: To dose to excess; to give an overdose, or too many doses, to. | Too great a dose; an excessive dose.
overgaze: To gaze; to overlook. (poetic) "Earth's o'ergazing mountains." Byron.
overharden: To harden too much; to make too hard. Boyle.
overhand: The upper hand; advantage; superiority; mastery. He had gotten thereby a great overhand on me. Sir T. More. | 1. (Sewing) Over and over; -- applied to a style of sewing, or to a seam, in which two edges, usually selvedges, are sewed together by passing each stitch over both. 2.
overpass: 1. To go over or beyond; to cross; as, to overpass a river; to overpass limits. 2. To pass over; to omit; to overlook; to disregard. All the beauties of the East He slightly viewed and slightly overpassed. Milton. 3. To surpass; to excel. R. Browning.
overfill: To fill to excess; to surcharge.
overbearing: 1. Overpowering; subduing; repressing. I. Watts. 2. Aggressively haughty; arrogant; domineering; tyrannical; dictatorial; insolent. --O`ver*bear"ing*ly, adv. -- O`ver*bear"ing*ness, n.
overhung: 1. Covered over; ornamented with hangings. Carlyle. 2. Suspended from above or from the top. Overhung door, a sliding door, suspended door, suspended from the top, as upon rollers.
overslaugh: A bar in a river; as, the overslaugh in the Hudson River. [Local, U. S.] Bartlett. | To hinder or stop, as by an overslaugh or an impediment; as, to overslaugh a bill in a legislative body; to overslaugh a military officer, that is, to hinder his promotion or employment.
overlead: To domineer over; to affront; to treat with indignity. (old) Chaucer.
ovatelanceolate: Having a form intermediate between ovate and lanceolate.
overget: 1. To reach; to overtake; to pass. (old) 2. To get beyond; to get over or recover from.
overweary: To weary too much; to tire out. Dryden.
overcoat: A coat worn over the other clothing; a greatcoat; a topcoat.
ovenbird: (a) Any species of the genus Furnarius, allied to the creepers. They inhabit South America and the West Indies, and construct curious oven-shaped nests. (b) In the United States, Seiurus aurocapillus; -- called also golden-crowned thrush. (c) In England, sometimes applied to the willow warbler, and to the long-tailed titmouse.
overwatch: 1. To watch too much. 2. To weary or exhaust by watching. Dryden.
overfreight: To put too much freight in or upon; to load too full, or too heavily; to overload.
overearnest: Too earnest. -- O"ver*ear"nest*ly, adv. -- O"ver*ear"nest*ness, n.
overburn: To burn too much; to be overzealous.
overtop: 1. To rise above the top of; to exceed in height; to tower above. "To old Pelion." Shak. 2. To go beyond; to transcend; to transgress. If kings presume to overtop the law by which they reign, . . . they are by law to be reduced into order. Milton. 3. To make of less importance, or throw into the background, by superior excellence; to dwarf; to obscure. Becon.
overlearned: Too learned. -- O"ver*learn"ed, adv. -- O"ver*learn"ed*ness, n.
overset: 1. To turn or tip (anything) over from an upright, or a proper, position so that it lies upon its side or bottom upwards; to upset; as, to overset a chair, a coach, a ship, or a building. Dryden. 2. | To turn, or to be turned, over; to be upset. Mortimer.
overshot: From Overshoot, v. t. Overshot wheel, a vertical water wheel, the circumference of which is covered with cavities or buckets, and which is turned by water which shoots over the top of it, filling the buckets on the farther side and acting chiefly by its we'ght.
overrun: 1. To run over; to grow or spread over in excess; to invade and occupy; to take possession of; as, the vine overran its trellis; the farm is overrun with witch grass. | 1. To run, pass, spread, or flow over or by something; to be beyond, or in excess. Despised and trodden down of all that overran. Spenser. 2. (Print.) To extend beyond its due or desired length;
overquell: To quell or subdue completely. Bp. Hall.
overweight: 1. Weight over and above what is required by law or custom. 2. Superabundance of weight; preponderance. | Overweighing; excessive. (old) "Of no overweight worth." Fuller.
overscented: 1. Scented excessively. 2. Covered or concealed by a different odor. Fuller.
overtrade: To trade beyond one's capital; to buy goods beyond the means of paying for or seleng them; to overstock the market.
overstory: The clearstory, or upper story, of a building.
overgive: To give over; to surrender; to yield. (old) Spenser.
overdue: Due and more than due; delayed beyond the proper time of arrival or payment, etc.; as, an overdue vessel; an overdue note.
overproud: Exceedingly or unduly proud. "Overproud of his victory." Milton.
overbuild: 1. To build over. Milton. 2. To build too much; to build beyond the demand.
overaffect: To affect or care for unduly. (old) Milton.
overready: Too ready. -- O"ver*read"*i*ly, adv. -- O"ver*read"i*ness, n.
overflourish: 1. To make excessive display or flourish of. Collier. 2. To embellish with outward ornaments or flourishes; to varnish over. (old) Shak.
overtone: One of the harmonics faintly heard with and above a tone as it dies away, produced by some aliquot portion of the vibrating sting or column of air which yields the fundamental tone; one of the natural harmonic scale of tones, as the octave, twelfth, fifteenth, etc.; an aliquot or "partial" tone; a harmonic. See Harmonic, and Tone. Tyndall.
overbid: To bid or offer beyond, or in excess of. Dryden.
overstand: To stand on the price or conditions of, so as to lose a sale; to lose by an extravagant price or hard conditions. (old) What madman would o'erstand his market twice Dryden.
overpersuade: To persuade or influence against one's inclination or judgment. Pope.
ovarious: Consisting of eggs; as, ovarious food. Thomson.
ovoidal: Resembling an egg in shape; egg-shaped; ovate; as, an ovoidal apple.
overreach: 1. To reach above or beyond in any direction. 2. To deceive, or get the better of, by artifice or cunning; to outwit; to cheat. Shak. | 1. To reach too far; as: (a) To strike the toe of the hind foot against the heel or shoe of the forefoot; -- said of horses. (b) (Naut.) To sail on one tack farther than is necessary. Shak. 2.
overburden: To load with too great weight or too much care, etc. Sir P. Sidney. | The waste which overlies good stone in a quarry. Raymond.
overbalance: 1. To exceed equality with; to outweigh. Locke. 2. To cause to lose balance or equilibrium. | Excess of weight or value; something more than an equivalent; as, an overbalance of exports. J. Edwards.
overagitate: To agitate or discuss beyond what is expedient. Bp. Hall.
overmeddling: Excessive interference. "Justly shent for their overmeddling." Fuller.
overhaul: 1. To haul or drag over; hence, to turn over for examination; to inspect; to examine thoroughly with a view to corrections or repairs. 2. (Naut.) To gain upon in a chase; to overtake. | A strict examination with a view to correction or repairs.
overly: 1. Careless; negligent; inattentive; superfical; not thorough. (old) Bp. Hall. 2. Excessive; too much. Coleridge.
overcapable: Too capable. Overcapable of such pleasing errors. Hooker.
overread: To read over, or peruse. Shak.
overrate: To rate or value too highly. | An excessive rate. Massinger.
ovulation: The formation of ova or eggs in the ovary, and the discharge of the same. In the mammalian female the discharge occurs during menstruation.
overeager: Too eager; too impatient. -- O`ver*ea"ger*ly, adv. -- O"ver*ea"ger*ness, n.
ovotesttis: An organ which produces both ova and spermatozoids; an hermaphrodite gland.
overtime: Time beyond, or in excess of, a limit; esp., extra working time.
overmaster: To overpower; to subdue; to vanquish; to govern.
overtempt: To tempt exceedingly, or beyond the power of resistance. Milton.
overmuchness: The quality or state of being in excess; superabundance. B. Jonson.
overdare: To dare too much or rashly; to be too daring.
overflowing: An overflow; that which overflows; exuberance; copiousness. He was ready to bestow the overflowings of his full mind on anybody who would start a subject. Macaulay.
overproportion: To make of too great proportion.
overfront: To confront; to oppose; to withstand. (old) Milton.
overseas: Over the sea; abroad. Milton. Tennyson.
overturnable: Capable of being, or liable to be, overturned or subverted.
overestimate: To estimate too highly; to overvalue. | An estimate that is too high; as, an overestimate of the vote.
ovation: 1. (Rom. Antiq.) A lesser kind of triumph allowed to a commander for an easy, bloodless victory, or a victory over slaves. 2. Hence: An expression of popular homage; the tribute of the multitude to a public favorite. To rain an April of ovation round Their statues. Tennyson.
overmeasure: To measure or estimate too largely. | Excessive measure; the excess beyond true or proper measure; surplus.
oviducal: Of or pertaining to oviducts; as, oviducal glands.
overfrieze: To cover with a frieze, or as with a frieze. E. Hall.
overload: To load or fill to excess; to load too heavily. | An excessive load; the excess beyond a proper load.
overply: To ply to excess; to exert with too much vigor; to overwork. Milton.
overshoe: A shoe that is worn over another for protection from wet or for extra warmth; esp., an India-rubber shoe; a galoche.
overlordship: Lordship or supremacy of a person or a people over others. J. R. Green.
overcrow: To crow, exult, or boast, over; to overpower. Spenser. Shak.
overwind: To wind too tightly, as a spring, or too far, as a hoisting rope on a drum.
oversight: 1. Watchful care; superintendence; general supervision. 2. An overlooking; an omission; an error. Hooker. 3. Escape from an overlooked peril. "His fool-happy oversight." Spenser. Syn. -- Superintendence; supervision; inspection; overlooking; inadvertence; neglect; mistake; error; omission.
overforward: Forward to excess; too forward. -- O"ver*for"ward*ness, n.
overmanner: In an excessive manner; excessively. (old) Wiclif.
oversleep: To sleep beyond; as, to oversleep one's self or one's usual hour of rising.
overslow: To render slow; to check; to curb. (old) Hammond.
overdrive: To drive too hard, or far, or beyond strength.
overshine: 1. To shine over or upon; to illumine. Shak. 2. To excel in shining; to outshine. Shak.
overswell: To swell or rise above; to overflow. Shak.
overvalue: 1. To value excessively; to rate at too high a price. "To overvalue human power." Holyday. 2. To exceed in value. H. Brooke.
ovipositing: The depositing of eggs, esp. by insects.
ovoid: Resembling an egg in shape; egg-shaped; ovate; as, an ovoidal apple. | A solid resembling an egg in shape.
overmost: Over the rest in authority; above all others; highest. (old) Fabyan.
ovateacuminate: Having an ovate form, but narrowed at the end into a slender point.
overskirt: An upper skirt, shorter than the dress, and usually draped.
ovatesubulate: Having an ovate form, but with a subulate tip or extremity.
overcarry: To carry too far; to carry beyond the proper point. Hayward.
overcanopy: To cover as with a canopy. Shak.
overheadcharges: Those general charges or expenses in any business which cannot be charged up as belonging exclusively to any particular part of the work or product, as where different kinds of goods are made, or where there are different departments in a business; -- called also fixed, establishment, or (in a manufacturing business) administration, selling, and distribution, charges, etc.
overcarking: Too anxious; too full of care. (old) Fuller.
overmorrow: The day after or following to-morrow. (old) Bible (1551).
overreacher: One who overreaches; one who cheats; a cheat.
oven: A place arched over with brick or stonework, and used for baking, heating, or drying; hence, any structure, whether fixed or portable, which may be heated for baking, drying, etc.; esp., now, a chamber in a stove, used for baking or roasting.
overtrow: To be too trustful or confident; to trust too much. (old) Wyclif
ovariole: One of the tubes of which the ovaries of most insects are composed.
overhele: To hele or cover over. (old) B. Jonson.
overwear: To wear too much; to wear out. Drayton.
overoffice: To domineer over by virtue of office. (old) Shak.
overanxious: Anxious in an excessive or needless degree. -- O"ver*anx"ious*ly, adv.
overlinger: To cause to linger; to detain too long. (old) Fuller.
overword: To say in too many words; to express verbosely. Hales.
oversee: 1. To superintend; to watch over; to direct; to look or see after; to overlook. 2. To omit or neglect seeing. Spenser. | To see too or too much; hence, to be deceived. (old) The most expert gamesters may sometimes oversee. Fuller. Your partiality to me is much overseen, if you think me fit to correct your Latin.
overplus: That which remains after a supply, or beyond a quantity proposed; surplus. Shak. "The overplus of a great fortune." Addison.
oversum: A sum or quantity over; surplus. (old) Holinshed.
overlayer: One who overlays; that with which anything is overlaid.
overtoil: To weary excessively; to exhaust. Then dozed a while herself, but overtoiled By that day's grief and travel. Tennyson.
overtire: To tire to excess; to exhaust. | To become too tired. Br. Hall.
overinfluence: To influence in an excessive degree; to have undue influence over.
overlie: To lie over or upon; specifically, to suffocate by lying upon; as, to overlie an infant. Quain. A woman by negligence overlieth her child in her sleeping. Chaucer.
overlanguaged: Employing too many words; diffuse. Lowell.
overpester: To pester exceedingly or excessively. Sir W. Raleigh.
overarm: Done (as bowling or pitching) with the arm raised above the shoulder. See Overhard. "An over-arm with a round-arm bowler." R. A. Proctor.
ovism: The old theory that the egg contains the whole embryo of the future organism and the germs of all subsequent offsprings and is merely awakened to activity by the spermatozoön; -- opposed to spermism or animalculism.
overconfidence: Excessive confidence; too great reliance or trust.
overfullness: The state of being excessively or abnormally full, so as to cause overflow, distention, or congestion; excess of fullness; surfeit.
overbulk: To oppress by bulk; to overtower. [Obs. & R.] Shak.
overdress: To dress or adorn to excess; to dress too much. Pope.
ovariotomist: One who performs, or is skilled in, ovariotomy.
overexquisite: Too exquisite; too exact or nice; too careful.
overact: 1. To act or perform to excess; to exaggerate in acting; as, he overacted his part. 2. To act upon, or influence, unduly. (old) The hope of inheritance overacts them. Milton. | To act more than is necessary; to go to excess in action. B. Jonson.
overlay: 1. To lay, or spread, something over or across; hence, to cover; to overwhelm; to press excessively upon. When any country is overlaid by the multitude which live upon it. Sir W. Raleigh. | 1. A covering. Sir W. Scott. 2. (Printing) A piece of paper pasted upon the tympan sheet to improve the impression by making it stronger at a particular place.
oval: 1. Of or pertaining to eggs; done in the egg, or inception; as, oval conceptions. (old) 2. Having the figure of an egg; oblong and curvilinear, with one end broader than the other, or with both ends… | A body or figure in the shape of an egg, or popularly, of an ellipse. Cassinian oval (Geom.), the locus of a point the product of whose distances from two fixed points is constant;
overhang: 1. To impend or hang over. Beau. & Fl. 2. To hang over; to jut or project over. Pope. | 1. In a general sense, that which just out or projects; a projection; also, the measure of the projection; as, the overhang is five feet. 2. Specifically: The projection of an upper part (as a roof,…
overawe: To awe exceedingly; to subjugate or restrain by awe or great fear. The king was present in person to overlook the magistrates, and overawe these subjects with the terror of his sword. Spenser.
overlander: One who travels over lands or countries; one who travels overland.
oversorrow: To grieve or afflict to excess. (old) Milton.
overland: Being, or accomplished, over the land, instead of by sea; as, an overland journey.
overruler: One who, or that which, controls, governs, or determines. Sir P. Sidney.
overmarch: To march too far, or too much; to exhaust by marching. Baker.
overlord: One who is lord over another or others; a superior lord; a master. Freeman.
overgo: 1. To travel over. Shak. 2. To exceed; to surpass. (old) Sir P. Sidney. 3. To cover. (old) Chapman. 4. To oppress; to weigh down. (old) Shak.
overslip: To slip or slide over; to pass easily or carelessly beyond; to omit; to neglect; as, to overslip time or opportunity.
overfree: Free to excess; too liberal; too familiar. -- O"ver*free"ly, adv.
overnight: The fore part of the night last past; the previous evening. Shak. | In the fore part of the night last past; in the evening before; also, during the night; as, the candle will not last overnight. I had been telling her all that happened overnight. Dickens.
overeat: 1. To gnaw all over, or on all sides. (old) Shak. 2. To eat to excess; -- often with a reflexive.
ovine: Of or pertaining to sheep; consisting of sheep.
overlook: 1. To look down upon from a place that is over or above; to look over or view from a higher position; to rise above, so as to command a view of; as, to overlook a valley from a hill. "The pile o'erlooked the town." Dryden. [Titan] with burning eye did hotly overlook them. Shak. 2. Hence: To supervise; to watch over; sometimes, to observe secretly;
overabound: To be exceedingly plenty or superabundant. Pope.
overpoise: To outweigh; to overbalance. Sir T. Browne. | Preponderant weight; a counterbalance. Mrs. Browning.
oviform: Having the form or figure of an egg; egg-shaped; as, an oviform leaf.
overleaven: To leaven too much; hence, to change excessively; to spoil. (old)
overempty: To make too empty; to exhaust. Carew.
overstock: To fill too full; to supply in excess; as, to overstock a market with goods, or a farm with cattle.
overscrupulousness: The quality or state of being overscrupulous; excess of scrupulousness.
overfly: To cross or pass over by flight. Byron.
overfatigue: To fatigue to excess; to tire out.
overquietness: Too much quietness. Sir. T. Browne.
overpraising: The act of praising unduly; excessive praise. Milton.
ovariotomy: The operation of removing one or both of the ovaries; oöphorectomy.
overlying: Lying over or upon something; as, overlying rocks.
oversay: To say over; to repeat. Ford.
overname: To name over or in a series; to recount. (old) Shak.
overstraitly: Too straitly or strictly. (old) Sir W. Raleigh.
overprize: Toprize excessively; to overvalue. Sir H. Wotton.
overshadower: One that throws a shade, or shadow, over anything. Bacon.
overpeer: To peer over; to rise above.
overt: 1. Open to view; public; apparent; manifest. Overt and apparent virtues bring forth praise. Bacon. 2. (Law) Not covert; open; public; manifest; as, an overt act of treason. Macaulay. No person shall be convicted of treason unless on the testimony of two witnesses to the same overt act, or on confession in open court. Constitution of the U. S.
overproof: Containing more alcohol than proof spirit; stronger than proof spirit; that is, containing more than 49.3 per cent by weight of alcohol.
overpay: To pay too much to; to reward too highly.
overtower: To tower over or above. | To soar too high. Fuller.
overcautious: Too cautious; cautious or prudent to excess. -- O"ver*cau"tious*ly, adv. -- O"ver*cau"tiou*ness, n.
overvote: To outvote; to outnumber in votes given. Eikon Basilike.
overspeak: To exceed in speaking; to speak too much; to use too many words.
overgrace: To grace or honor exceedingly or beyond desert. Beau. & Fl.
overture: 1. An opening or aperture; a recess; a recess; a chamber. (old) Spenser. "The cave's inmost overture." Chapman. 2. Disclosure; discovery; revelation. (old) It was he That made the overture of thy… | To make an overture to; as, to overture a religious body on some subject.
ovatecylindraceous: Having a form intermediate between ovate and cylindraceous.
overchange: Too much or too frequent change; fickleness. Beau. & Fl.
overstay: To stay beyond the time or the limits of; as, to overstay the appointed time. Bp. Hall.
ovum: 1. (Biol.) A more or less spherical and transparent mass of granular protoplasm, which by a process of multiplication and growth develops into a mass of cells, constituting a new individual like the parent; an egg, spore, germ, or germ cell. See Illust. of Mycropyle. Note: The ovum is a typical cell, with a cell wall, cell substance, nucleus, and nucleolus.
overanxiety: The state of being overanxious; excessive anxiety.
overwrest: To wrest or force from the natural or proper position. Shak.
ovalbumin: The albumin from white of eggs; egg albumin; -- in distinction from serum albumin. See Albumin.
oviposition: The depositing of eggs, esp. by insects.
overawful: Awful, or reverential, in an excessive degree. Milton.
overman: 1. One in authority over others; a chief; usually, an overseer or boss. 2. An arbiter. 3. In the philosophy of Nietzsche, a man of superior physique and powers capable of dominating others; one fitted to survive in an egoistic struggle for the mastery.
overspread: To spread over; to cover; as, the deluge overspread the earth. Chaucer. Those nations of the North Which overspread the world. Drayton. | To be spread or scattered over.
overeye: 1. To superintend; to oversee; to inspect. (old) 2. To see; to observe. (old) Shak.
overboil: To boil over or unduly. Nor is discontent to keep the mind Deep in its fountain, lest it overboil In the hot throng. Byron.
overleap: To leap over or across; hence, to omit; to ignore. "Let me o'erleap that custom." Shak.
overwet: Excessive wetness. (old) Another ill accident is, overwet at sowing time. Bacon.
overworn: Worn out or subdued by toil; worn out so as to be trite.
oversow: To sow where something has already been sown. His enemy came and oversowed cockle among the wheat. Matt. x
overpost: To post over; to pass over swiftly, as by post. Shak.
overbrow: To hang over like a brow; to impend over. (poetic) Longfellow. Did with a huge projection overbrow Large space beneath. Wordsworth.
overexcitement: Excess of excitement; the state of being overexcited.
overlade: To load with too great a cargo; to overburden; to overload. Spenser.
overdraw: 1. To exaggerate; to overdo. 2. (Banking) To make drafts upon or against, in excess of the proper amount or limit.
ovoviviparous: Oviparous, but hatching the egg while it is within the body, as some fishes and reptiles.
ovicyst: The pouch in which incubation takes place in some Tunicata.
overcast: 1. To cast or cover over; hence, to cloud; to darken. Those clouds that overcast your morn shall fly. Dryden. 2. To compute or rate too high. Bacon. 3. (Sewing) To take long, loose stitches over (the raw edges of a seam) to prevent raveling.
overwise: Too wise; affectedly wise. -- O`ver*wise"ly, adv. -- O`ver*wise"ness, n.
overalls: 1. A kind of loose trousers worn over others to protect them from soiling. 2. Waterproof leggings. R. D. Blackmore.
overissue: An excessive issue; an issue, as of notes or bonds, exceeding the limit of capital, credit, or authority. An overissue of government paper. Brougham.
oviparous: Producing young from rggs; as, an oviparous animal, in which the egg is generally separated from the animal, and hatched after exclusion; -- opposed to viviparous.
overshake: To shake over or away; to drive away; to disperse. (old) Chaucer.
overboard: Over the side of a ship; hence, from on board of a ship, into the water; as, to fall overboard. To throw overboard, to discard; to abandon, as a dependent or friend.
oversize: To cover with viscid matter. O'ersized with coagulate gore. Shak.
overgloom: To spread gloom over; to make gloomy; to overshadow. Overgloomed by memories of sorrow. De Quincey.
oversoul: The all-containing soul. That unity, that oversout, within which every man's particular being is contained and made one with all other. Emerson.
ovipositor: The organ with which many insects and some other animals deposit their eggs. Some ichneumon files have a long ovipositor fitted to pierce the eggs or larvæ of other insects, in order to lay their own eggs within the same.
overrake: To rake over, or sweep across, from end to end, as waves that break over a vessel anchored with head to the sea.
overwhelm: 1. To cover over completely, as by a great wave; to overflow and bury beneath; to ingulf; hence, figuratively, to immerse and bear down; to overpower; to crush; to bury; to oppress, etc., overpoweringly. The sea overwhelmed their enemies. Ps. lxxviii. 53. Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and horror hath overwhelmed me. Ps. lv. 5.
overstep: To step over or beyond; to transgress. Shak.
overweather: To expose too long to the influence of the weather. (old) Shak.
oversupply: An excessive supply. A general oversupply or excess of all commodities. J. S. Mill.
overpress: 1. To bear upon with irresistible force; to crush; to overwhelm. Shak. 2. To overcome by importunity. Johnson.
overpressure: Excessive pressure or urging. London Athenæum.
overheadexpenses: Those general charges or expenses in any business which cannot be charged up as belonging exclusively to any particular part of the work or product, as where different kinds of goods are made, or where there are different departments in a business; -- called also fixed, establishment, or (in a manufacturing business) administration, selling, and distribution, charges, etc.
overspin: To spin out to too great length; to protract unduly. W. Cartwright.
overbear: 1. To bear down or carry down, as by excess of weight, power, force, etc.; to overcome; to suppress. The point of reputation, when the news first came of the battle lost, did overbear the reason of… | To bear fruit or offspring to excess; to be too prolific.
overweening: Unduly confident; arrogant; presumptuous; conceited. -- O`ver*ween"ingly, adv. Milton. -- O`ver*ween"ing*ness, n. Here's an overweening rogue. Shak.
